sections.name: General Knowledge / Current Affairs of India and Goa

p1.title: Passage 1
paras: Modern life treats sleep as a negotiable expense, the first item to be trimmed when work, study or entertainment demands more hours. Students boast of all-night revision and professionals of surviving on five hours, as though wakefulness were a form of virtue. The science of sleep tells a less flattering story. During sleep the brain consolidates the day's learning, clearing away metabolic waste and strengthening the connections that turn experience into memory. Hormones that regulate appetite and blood sugar are recalibrated, and the immune system performs much of its repair work. A person who is chronically short of sleep does not simply feel tired; he thinks more slowly, judges risks less accurately and becomes more vulnerable to infection, obesity and disorders of mood.

What makes the problem difficult is that its victims are poor judges of their own condition. After several nights of restricted sleep, people's performance on tests of attention continues to decline even as their sense of how impaired they are levels off. They adapt to feeling tired, and mistake the adaptation for recovery. Screens glowing late into the night, long commutes and shift work all conspire against rest. Treating sleep as a pillar of health, alongside diet and exercise, would require not only personal discipline but schools, employers and cities willing to respect the hours that the body requires.

p2.title: Passage 2
paras: We tend to imagine memory as a kind of recording, stored somewhere in the brain and played back, more or less faithfully, when we need it. Research over several decades suggests a different picture. A memory, it appears, is rebuilt each time it is recalled, assembled from fragments and filled out with what seems likely, what we have since learned and what others have told us. In well-known experiments, people who watched a film of a minor road accident and were later asked how fast the cars were going when they 'smashed' into each other gave higher estimates than those asked about cars that 'hit' each other; some in the first group even recalled broken glass that had never appeared.

None of this means that memory is useless. For most purposes it serves us well, and its flexibility allows us to generalise from experience rather than drown in detail. But it does mean that confidence is a poor guide to accuracy. A witness may be entirely sincere and entirely wrong, and the act of repeatedly questioning someone can shape the very recollection being sought. Institutions that rely on testimony, such as courts and inquiries, have reason to treat memory with respect but not with blind trust, and to question witnesses in ways that do not supply the answers.

questions.q: Which of the following best states the theme of the passage?
opts: Sleep is an essential biological need that modern habits wrongly treat as dispensable.
All-night study is an efficient way to prepare for examinations.
Diet and exercise matter more to health than sleep.
Screens are the sole cause of sleep loss in modern society.
questions.why: Main idea: modern life treats sleep 'as a negotiable expense', while science shows its many vital functions.

questions.q: According to the passage, during sleep the brain:
opts: consolidates the day's learning and clears away metabolic waste.
shuts down completely to save energy.
forgets most of what was learned that day.
raises appetite to prepare for the next day.
questions.why: Detail: 'the brain consolidates the day's learning, clearing away metabolic waste'.

questions.q: It can be inferred that a student who feels fine after a week of five-hour nights:
opts: will perform better than students who sleep longer.
has shown that boasts about little sleep are justified.
has fully adapted and no longer needs more sleep.
may still be significantly impaired without realising it.
questions.why: Inference: performance 'continues to decline even as their sense of how impaired they are levels off'; people 'mistake the adaptation for recovery'.

questions.q: The author's attitude towards people who boast of surviving on little sleep is:
opts: sceptical, regarding their pride as misplaced.
questions.why: Tone: they act 'as though wakefulness were a form of virtue', and 'the science of sleep tells a less flattering story'.

questions.q: As used in the passage, 'conspire against' means:
opts: combine to produce an unfavourable effect on
questions.why: Vocabulary: screens, commutes and shift work together work against rest; no actual plotting is meant.

questions.q: The main idea of the passage is that:
opts: Memory is an accurate recording that can be replayed at will.
Memory is reconstructed at each recall, so testimony must be handled with care.
Road accidents are usually misreported by the police.
Courts should stop relying on witnesses altogether.
questions.why: Main idea: 'A memory... is rebuilt each time it is recalled'; institutions should treat it 'with respect but not with blind trust'.

questions.q: Participants asked about cars that 'smashed' into each other:
opts: Refused to estimate the speed of the cars.
Gave lower speed estimates than the other group.
Recalled the film more accurately than the other group.
Gave higher speed estimates, and some recalled broken glass that was not there.
questions.why: Detail: they 'gave higher estimates' and 'some... even recalled broken glass that had never appeared'.

questions.q: It can be inferred that a witness who is confident about what he saw:
opts: May nevertheless give an inaccurate account.
Should not be allowed to testify.
questions.why: Inference: 'confidence is a poor guide to accuracy. A witness may be entirely sincere and entirely wrong'.

questions.q: The author's attitude towards human memory is best described as:
opts: Despairing of any reliable knowledge of the past.
Measured: valuing its usefulness while warning against over-reliance.
questions.why: Tone: 'None of this means that memory is useless... it serves us well', yet it deserves 'respect but not... blind trust'.

questions.q: As used in the passage, "sincere" in "entirely sincere and entirely wrong" means:
questions.why: Vocabulary: the contrast with 'entirely wrong' shows sincerity concerns honest belief, not accuracy.

questions.q: Choose the meaning of the idiom “under the weather”:
questions.why: 'Under the weather' means feeling slightly ill. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: Choose the one word for: “Able to use both hands equally well”
questions.why: Ambidextrous means equally skilled with the right and left hand. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: Choose the word closest in meaning to “reticent”:
questions.why: 'Reticent' means unwilling to speak freely; reserved. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: “I would rather ____ at home than go out in this rain.”
questions.why: 'Would rather' takes the bare infinitive. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: Select the correct indirect speech: He said to me, “I am leaving now; will you join me?”
opts: He told me that he is leaving now and asked if I would join him.
He told me that he was leaving then and asked whether I will join him.
He said me that he was leaving then and asked would I join him.
He told me that he was leaving then and asked if I would join him.
questions.why: Mixed sentences use 'told' for the statement and 'asked if' for the question; 'now' becomes 'then'. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: INS Sahyadri took part in Exercise INDRA 2026 at Vladivostok. INDRA is held between India and:
questions.why: The exercise ran from 13 to 18 October. Oct 2026.

questions.q: Which Union Territory launched India's first high-altitude wildlife safari, focused on snow leopard habitats in Rumbak, Shang and Uley?
opts: Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu
questions.why: The safari runs with specially designed vehicles in and around Hemis National Park. Oct 2026.

questions.q: The humanoid robot to fly on Gaganyaan's first uncrewed mission (G1) is named:
questions.why: ISRO completed crew-module and service-module separation tests at VSSC. Oct 2026.

questions.q: The Mukhyamantri Export Incentive Scheme announced in Goa's Budget 2026-27 supports:
opts: MSMEs, with up to ₹4 lakh a year for two years
questions.why: Meant for 50 MSMEs on a first-come-first-serve basis. Mar 2026.

questions.q: NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, launched in August 2026, will operate at:
questions.why: Launched on a Falcon Heavy from Kennedy Space Center on 30 August. Aug 2026.

questions.q: Which country was announced as the Guest Country of the 57th International Film Festival of India (Goa, November 2026)?
questions.why: Agreed under the Spain–India Dual Year 2026; Japan was Country of Focus at IFFI 2025. Jan 2026.

questions.q: ICMR's first High Altitude Medicine and Public Health Research Centre, whose foundation stone was laid in October 2026, is at:
questions.why: Laid by J. P. Nadda; partners include AFMS and AIIMS Bilaspur. Oct 2026.

questions.q: The present law governing village panchayats in Goa is the Goa Panchayat Raj Act of:
questions.why: It was framed after the 73rd Amendment.

questions.q: Who was the first Governor of Goa after it became a state in 1987?
questions.why: Before 1987 Goa, Daman and Diu had Lieutenant Governors.

questions.q: After the RBI's October 2026 policy, the Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) rate and Bank Rate stood at:
questions.why: Repo went to 5.50%, SDF to 5.25% and MSF/Bank Rate to 5.75%. Oct 2026.

questions.q: What comes next in the series? 4, 12, 36, 108, 324, …
questions.why: Each term is multiplied by 3. Next: 972. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: Ajay walks 6 km East, then turns left and walks 8 km. How far is Ajay from the starting point?
questions.why: The two legs are at right angles: √(6² + 8²) = 10 km. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: In a row of 34 students, Pooja is 9th from the left and Kiran is 16th from the right. How many students sit between them?
questions.why: Between them = 34 − (9 + 16) = 9. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: What is the angle between the hands of a clock at 9:30?
questions.why: Angle = |30×9 − 5.5×30| = 105°. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: The present ages of Vijay and Rekha are in the ratio 2 : 5. After 10 years the ratio will be 8 : 15. What is Rekha's present age?
questions.why: Let the ages be 2k and 5k: (2k + 10)/(5k + 10) = 8/15 gives k = 7, so Rekha is 35. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: What is the angle between the hands of a clock at 7:45?
questions.why: Angle = |30×7 − 5.5×45| = 37.5°. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: In a group of 110 people, 57 like Hindi, 72 like English and 24 like neither. How many like only Hindi?
questions.why: Both = 57 + 72 − (110 − 24) = 43; only Hindi = 57 − 43 = 14. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: If TABLET is written as UCEPJZ in a certain code, how is HEALTH written in that code?
questions.why: In the code the 1st letter moves 1 place, the 2nd 2 places, the 3rd 3 places, and so on: HEALTH → IGDPYN. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: What comes next in the series? 3, 7, 15, 27, 43, …
questions.why: The differences go up by 4 each time (4, 8, 12, 16, 20). Next: 63. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: Statements: Some doctors are teachers. No teachers are singers. Conclusions: I. No singers are doctors. II. Some doctors are not singers.
questions.why: Checked against every possible diagram of the statements: I need not be true, II must be true. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: Hahnemann held (§119) that one medicine can never be a substitute (succedaneum) for another because:
opts: medicines from the same family act alike
only the dose decides the action
substitutes are forbidden by the law of potency
every medicine has its own peculiar and distinct action
questions.why: §119: as every plant species differs, each medicine has a distinct action, so none can replace another.

questions.q: According to §138, the changes of health that a prover feels during the action of the medicine are:
opts: to be regarded as derived solely from that medicine
to be ignored unless they are new to him
to be regarded as his own latent disease
to be recorded only if confirmed in animals
questions.why: §138: all sufferings and changes during the proving, under proper conditions, belong to the medicine and are recorded as its symptoms.

questions.q: According to Kent's ninth observation, what does a well-conducted proving generally do to a healthy prover?
opts: It makes the prover more susceptible to all diseases
It has no effect when high potencies are used
questions.why: Kent's ninth observation: provers in good health are usually benefited, and sensitive provers may even be cured of latent troubles, by careful provings.

questions.q: Aconitum napellus is commonly known as:
questions.why: Aconitum napellus (Ranunculaceae) is monkshood or wolf's bane; deadly nightshade is Belladonna, foxglove Digitalis and thorn apple Stramonium.

questions.q: Rheumatism of the right shoulder (deltoid), so that the arm cannot be raised, is characteristic of:
questions.why: Sanguinaria: rheumatism of the right shoulder and deltoid, cannot raise the arm (Boericke).

questions.q: Diarrhoea before and during the menses, with the menstrual flow only at night or early morning, is characteristic of:
questions.why: Bovista (Boericke): diarrhoea before and during menses; flow only at night or early in the morning.

questions.q: The abbreviation 'gtt.' on a prescription stands for:
questions.why: Gtt. is short for guttae, drops.

questions.q: Under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, a drug sold under the name of another drug, or falsely claiming to be made by a certain manufacturer, is termed:
questions.why: Section 17-B defines spurious drugs (imitations and false claims of identity or maker); 17 covers misbranding and 17-A adulteration.

questions.q: The Synthesis repertory is essentially:
opts: a translation of Boenninghausen's Therapeutic Pocket Book
a repertory of general symptoms only, in three volumes
a card repertory for mechanical elimination
an enlarged and corrected Kent's Repertory, with additions from many sources and author references
questions.why: Synthesis builds on Kent's 6th edition with corrections, additions and source references; the three-volume generals-only work is Barthel and Klunker's Synthetic Repertory.

questions.q: In Kent's Repertory, the time sub-rubrics are listed in the order:
opts: morning, forenoon, noon, afternoon, evening, night, midnight
evening, night, midnight, morning, forenoon, noon, afternoon
night, midnight, morning, forenoon, noon, afternoon, evening
questions.why: Kent lists time through the day starting from morning and ending with night and midnight (and after midnight).

questions.q: Cerebrospinal fluid is mainly produced by the:
questions.why: The choroid plexuses secrete CSF; arachnoid granulations absorb it into the venous sinuses.

questions.q: In the WHO oral glucose tolerance test, an adult is given:
questions.why: The standard OGTT uses 75 g of anhydrous glucose; a 2-hour value of 200 mg/dL or more indicates diabetes.

questions.q: On a standard ECG recorded at 25 mm/s, the R–R interval is 4 large squares. The heart rate is about:
questions.why: Each large square is 0.2 s; heart rate = 300 ÷ number of large squares = 300 ÷ 4 = 75/min.

questions.q: Hepatitis D virus can cause infection only in the presence of:
questions.why: HDV is a defective RNA virus that needs HBsAg for its envelope, so it occurs only as co-infection or superinfection with HBV.

questions.q: The total leucocyte count in uncomplicated typhoid fever typically shows:
questions.why: Typhoid characteristically causes leucopenia with relative lymphocytosis and absent eosinophils; leucocytosis suggests a complication such as perforation.

questions.q: Prolonged bleeding time with a low platelet count but normal PT and aPTT in an otherwise well child after a viral illness suggests:
questions.why: Isolated thrombocytopenia prolongs bleeding time while coagulation tests stay normal; haemophilia prolongs aPTT, and vitamin K deficiency and DIC prolong PT.

questions.q: Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord is caused by deficiency of:
questions.why: B12 deficiency damages the dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts, causing loss of joint position and vibration sense with spastic weakness.

questions.q: A thin, breathless COPD patient with pursed-lip breathing, a hyperinflated chest and near-normal blood gases until late is described as a:
questions.why: Emphysema-dominant patients hyperventilate to keep oxygenation ('pink puffers'); bronchitis-dominant patients are hypoxic, cyanosed and oedematous ('blue bloaters').

questions.q: A gastric ulcer that is round and 'punched out', with pain felt in a small spot, calls for:
questions.why: Kali bich has deep, round, punched-out ulcers on mucous membranes and pains in small spots that can be covered with a fingertip.

questions.q: A baby normally begins to smile socially (in response to a face) at about:
questions.why: The social smile appears at 6–8 weeks; it is a key early social milestone.

questions.q: Meigs' syndrome is ascites and right-sided hydrothorax associated with:
opts: a granulosa cell tumour of the uterus
questions.why: Classic Meigs' syndrome is a benign ovarian fibroma with ascites and pleural effusion that resolve after removal.

questions.q: The first aid to stop external bleeding from a limb wound is:
opts: washing the wound with hot water
applying a cold drink to the lips
firm direct pressure over the wound with a clean pad
questions.why: Direct pressure with elevation stops most external haemorrhage; a tourniquet is a last resort.

questions.q: The specific antidote for paracetamol overdose is:
questions.why: N-acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione and prevents liver necrosis.

questions.q: The secondary attack rate is mainly a measure of:
opts: the case fatality of a disease
the infectiousness (communicability) of a disease among susceptible contacts
the virulence of the agent in the index case
the total burden of disease in the community
questions.why: Secondary attack rate = cases among contacts within one incubation period / susceptible contacts; Park uses it to measure communicability.

questions.q: Under Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK), children are screened for defects at birth, diseases, deficiencies and:
questions.why: RBSK screens children aged 0-18 years for the '4 Ds': defects at birth, diseases, deficiencies and developmental delays including disability.
